bibl.title: Recalibration of Auditory Space following Milliseconds of Cross-Modal Discrepancy

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how quickly the auditory spatial map is recalibrated by conflicting visual information, and whether accumulated evidence of error is required to trigger it
span.quote: Nonetheless, the dynamics of sensory recalibration is unknown, and it is unclear whether prolonged inconsistency is required to trigger recalibration or whether such mechanisms are continuously engaged in self-maintenance.

span.label: is cross-sensory recalibration engaged from the first discrepancy, or only after repeated and consistent error
span.quote: The extant data on sensory recalibration observed after extensive exposure are consistent with the following two competing hypotheses about the underlying mechanism: (1) a mechanism that becomes engaged from the onset of exposure to the discrepancy; and (2) a mechanism that requires accumulation of evidence of error in the form of repeated and consistent discrepancy before it becomes engaged.

span.label: shows the auditory spatial map shifts after a single 35 ms exposure to an audiovisual discrepancy, so recalibration is continuously operational rather than triggered by accumulated error
span.quote: We show that in humans recalibration of perceived auditory space by vision can occur after a single exposure to discrepant auditory–visual stimuli lasting only a few milliseconds.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We show that in humans recalibration of perceived auditory space by vision can occur after a single exposure to discrepant auditory–visual stimuli lasting only a few milliseconds.

span.label: visual recalibration of auditory space
span.quote: We investigated auditory spatial recalibration by vision.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: On unisensory auditory (A) trials, subjects reported the location of sound, on unisensory visual (V) trials, they reported the location of visual stimulus, and on bisensory (AV) trials they reported both the location of visual stimulus and location of auditory stimulus.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Vision acts as a teaching signal that corrects the auditory spatial map because visual location estimates are far more reliable (lower response variance) than auditory ones, producing self-supervised learning without external feedback
span.quote: It seems that vision provided a teaching signal for auditory recalibration because the visual estimates were much more reliable (much lower variance in responses) ( Burge et al., 2010 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Perceived unity of the two signals plus the size of the discrepancy jointly gate recalibration, so a sizable map shift happens only when the conflict is likely to reflect systematic error rather than noise, which keeps the perceptual system stable
span.quote: Therefore, the dependency of recalibration on the perceived unity of the signals as well as its dependence on the degree of discrepancy together suggests that a sizable shift in the auditory map does not occur all the time and is selective to situations wherein the discrepancy likely reflects a systematic error in one of the modalities.

span.label: the field's default position is diagnosed as an artefact of which experiments existed: no one had tested single exposures, so the accumulation account won implicitly
span.quote: To date, the lack of evidence for fast recalibration has implicitly favored the latter hypothesis.

span.label: the experiment is not built but found - pseudorandom interleaving in a dataset collected for another question makes every auditory trial's predecessor a single-exposure manipulation
span.quote: The raw data from these spatial localization judgments have been used in another study ( Wozny et al., 2010 ).

span.label: two accounts that agree on most trials are separated by isolating the subset where they predict opposite directions
span.quote: We scrutinized this issue further by examining the subset of trials in which a shift in the direction of visual discrepancy and a shift in the direction of visual stimulus would be in opposite directions.

span.label: the dependent measure is defined relative to each observer's own average response to that sound position, so a shift of zero is what randomness would give
span.quote: Thus, if the distribution of responses to a given sound position is sampled randomly, on average this shift in perceived auditory location would be zero. Therefore, any average shift that significantly deviates from zero would indicate a dependence on the independent variable ( Fig. 1 b–d , abscissa).

span.label: the preceding-auditory-trial condition serves as the control that a general response bias would also have produced, and it shows nothing
span.quote: There was not a significant effect of previous auditory location on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 651, p > 0.05, n = 126, 126, 133, 132, and 135 for the five locations).

span.label: an unmeasured variable - whether the two stimuli were perceived as one event - is recovered indirectly from the spatial judgments themselves
span.quote: Because we did not ask observers to report their perception of unity/independence, we indirectly identified these trials based on observer's spatial judgments.

span.label: the cutoff defining that inferred variable is disclosed as arbitrary and checked for robustness
span.quote: We left out the remaining A trials due to the possibility that small differences in reported locations may be due to motor errors; however, results remain qualitatively the same using other cutoff values.

span.label: the decay of the effect is traced by stepping back through the trial history rather than by a separate experiment
span.quote: As expected, the recalibration effect is degraded the further back we look in the AV history of trials, as intervening AV discrepancies counteract the effect.

span.label: accumulation is measured by finding runs of consecutive same-direction discrepancies that the randomisation happened to produce
span.quote: As can be seen in Figure 4 b , the degree of shift in the auditory spatial map increases with the number of repetitions of discrepancies in the same direction.

span.label: the paper names the possibility that its own randomised design created the plasticity it reports
span.quote: It is also conceivable that exposure to randomly varying discrepancies across trials in this experiment induced the nervous system to enter a “plastic state,” thus resulting a higher rate of recalibration than usual.

span.label: the stability objection is answered by the unity dependence: large shifts happen only when the signals are taken to share a source, which is when a discrepancy implies a real error
span.quote: Therefore, the dependency of recalibration on the perceived unity of the signals as well as its dependence on the degree of discrepancy together suggests that a sizable shift in the auditory map does not occur all the time and is selective to situations wherein the discrepancy likely reflects a systematic error in one of the modalities.

span.label: A response-level (rather than perceptual) account of the visual bias cannot be ruled out.
span.quote: The absence of an effect of previous sound position on current auditory response suggests that the observed visual bias may not be a simple response bias; however, it is possible that the response bias is stronger following visual trials due to a higher confidence in response or the higher saliency of stimuli on those trials.

span.label: The reason the effect fails to cross the midline is undetermined.
span.quote: Additional analyses suggest that the recalibration effect does not transfer across hemifields (data not shown); however, it is not clear whether this reflects a midline boundary effect or a general degradation of the effect across space.

span.label: Perceived unity was inferred from spatial judgements rather than reported by observers.
span.quote: Because we did not ask observers to report their perception of unity/independence, we indirectly identified these trials based on observer's spatial judgments.

span.label: The trajectory of recalibration over repeated exposures needs a dedicated, larger and blocked design.
span.quote: Future studies should further explore the dynamics of recalibration using repetition of the exact discrepancy, with larger sample sizes and additional number of repetitions, both in randomly interleaving and blocked designs to provide a clearer description of the trajectory.

span.label: the visual-location bias cannot be shown to be perceptual rather than a decision-level response bias
span.quote: The absence of a similar effect induced by a preceding auditory stimulus ( Fig. 1 c ) makes a general response bias explanation less likely; however, this explanation cannot be ruled out.

span.label: why vision teaches audition and not the reverse is undecided between reliability weighting and a fixed teacher role
span.quote: However, it is also possible that for each perceptual dimension (e.g., space), one modality (e.g., vision) enjoys the hardwired status of teacher regardless of the quality of the signal at any given time.

span.label: the randomly varying discrepancies may themselves have induced an unusually plastic state
span.quote: It is also conceivable that exposure to randomly varying discrepancies across trials in this experiment induced the nervous system to enter a “plastic state,” thus resulting a higher rate of recalibration than usual.

span.label: whether the shift is capped or the learning rate slows is not resolved
span.quote: This could be due to a hardwired cap on the degree of change in these basic maps, or alternatively, due to a slowing down of the learning rate. As can be seen in Figure 4 b , the degree of shift in the auditory spatial map increases with the number of repetitions of discrepancies in the same direction, but the rate of accumulation appears to slow down, suggesting a decrease in learning rate.

span.label: perception of unity was never asked for and had to be inferred from the responses
span.quote: Because we did not ask observers to report their perception of unity/independence, we indirectly identified these trials based on observer's spatial judgments.

span.label: the teaching signal and self-supervised learning, imported to describe one modality correcting another with no external feedback
span.quote: The visual signal appears to serve as a teaching signal for auditory modality, resulting in self-supervised learning of sensory representations.

span.label: the trial-by-trial adaptation-to-induced-error paradigm, imported as the expected timescale that sensory maps were assumed not to share
span.quote: However, an important difference between motor adaptation and the current example of sensory adaptation is that in the former, direct feedback can be used as teaching signal. Moreover, the motor system is expected to be highly malleable and dynamic (for instance, due to muscle fatigue), and thus, subject to adjustment.

span.label: recalibration - as a slow developmental or post-injury repair process versus as a continuously running self-maintenance mechanism; the paper moves the term from the first to the second
span.quote: Therefore, sensory recalibration has traditionally been associated with compensation for permanent changes that would occur during development or after traumatic injuries or stroke.

span.label: the shift in perceived sound location - as a bias toward the absolute location of the seen stimulus versus as a shift of the auditory map in the direction of the discrepancy; the two coincide on most trials and are separated only on a designed subset
span.quote: We scrutinized this issue further by examining the subset of trials in which a shift in the direction of visual discrepancy and a shift in the direction of visual stimulus would be in opposite directions.

span.label: bias - response bias at the decision level versus perceptual bias as a prior expectation; the data cannot separate them
span.quote: This bias could reflect a response bias (i.e., decision level) or a perceptual bias (i.e., prior expectation of an even at a given position).

span.label: perception versus learning - a distinction the result is said to blur, since a single 35 ms exposure changes a perceptual map
span.quote: These findings blur the distinction between perception and learning.

span.label: adaptation - motor, where an error signal is directly fed back, versus sensory, where one modality must serve as the teacher
span.quote: However, an important difference between motor adaptation and the current example of sensory adaptation is that in the former, direct feedback can be used as teaching signal. Moreover, the motor system is expected to be highly malleable and dynamic (for instance, due to muscle fatigue), and thus, subject to adjustment.

span.label: why vision teaches audition - because its estimates are more reliable here, or because it holds the teacher role regardless of signal quality; two senses of a modality being dominant
span.quote: However, it is also possible that for each perceptual dimension (e.g., space), one modality (e.g., vision) enjoys the hardwired status of teacher regardless of the quality of the signal at any given time.

span.label: builds-on → Wozny et al., 2010
span.quote: The raw data from these spatial localization judgments have been used in another study ( Wozny et al., 2010 ).

span.label: extends → McLaughlin, 1967; Redding and Wallace, 2003; Thoroughman et al., 2007 (motor adaptation)
span.quote: The fast recalibration in the present study resembles those previously reported in motor adaptation studies, during which recalibration of movements are found to occur within a few trials of artificially induced error ( McLaughlin, 1967 ; Redding and Wallace, 2003 ; Thoroughman et al., 2007 ).

span.label: contradicts → Hofman et al., 1998; Zwiers et al., 2003 (sensory recalibration as slow, long-term adjustment)
span.quote: Previous studies of sensory recalibration have reinforced this notion ( Hofman et al., 1998 ; Zwiers et al., 2003 ), therefore, sensory recalibration has traditionally been regarded as a process for adjusting to long-term changes such as those occurring during development or after a permanent damage from injury or stroke.

span.label: contradicts → the accumulation hypothesis, that recalibration requires repeated and consistent evidence of error before engaging
span.quote: The extant data on sensory recalibration observed after extensive exposure are consistent with the following two competing hypotheses about the underlying mechanism: (1) a mechanism that becomes engaged from the onset of exposure to the discrepancy; and (2) a mechanism that requires accumulation of evidence of error in the form of repeated and consistent discrepancy before it becomes engaged.

span.label: critiques → the inference from absent evidence to the accumulation account, which the field had made implicitly
span.quote: To date, the lack of evidence for fast recalibration has implicitly favored the latter hypothesis.

span.label: extends → ventriloquist-aftereffect studies using hundreds or thousands of exposures at a fixed discrepancy
span.quote: In contrast to motor or sensorimotor adaptation, which can be relatively rapid, cross-sensory recalibration (the change in an isolated sensory representation after exposure to conflicting cross-modal information) has been reported only as a result of an extensive amount of exposure to sensory discrepancy (e.g., hundreds or thousands of trials, or prolonged durations).

span.label: contradicts → the view that spatial and temporal maps are foundational and therefore stable
span.quote: In contrast, spatial and temporal maps are considered foundational to all perceptual processes and are expected to be fairly stable.

span.label: supports → reliability-weighted accounts of cross-modal dominance
span.quote: It seems that vision provided a teaching signal for auditory recalibration because the visual estimates were much more reliable (much lower variance in responses) ( Burge et al., 2010 ).

span.label: builds-on → motor adaptation studies showing recalibration within a few trials of induced error
span.quote: However, an important difference between motor adaptation and the current example of sensory adaptation is that in the former, direct feedback can be used as teaching signal. Moreover, the motor system is expected to be highly malleable and dynamic (for instance, due to muscle fatigue), and thus, subject to adjustment.

span.label: AV discrepancy —causes→ auditory spatial map
span.quote: The results show that shift in perceived auditory location is in the direction of visual discrepancy. This confirms that the observed change in auditory localization is driven by preceding auditory–visual discrepancy (or “error”), thus indicating visual recalibration of auditory space (rather than a bias toward the exposed absolute visual location).

span.label: ventriloquist aftereffect —is-a→ cross-sensory recalibration
span.quote: It has been known that after repeated exposure to simultaneous but spatially discrepant auditory and visual stimuli, the perceived location of a solitary auditory stimulus is shifted in the direction of the previously experienced visual stimuli ( Canon, 1970 ; Radeau and Bertelson, 1974 ; Recanzone, 1998 ; Lewald, 2002 )—a phenomenon often referred to as the “ventriloquist aftereffect.”

span.label: response bias —distinct-from→ perceptual bias
span.quote: This bias could reflect a response bias (i.e., decision level) or a perceptual bias (i.e., prior expectation of an even at a given position).

span.label: perception of unity —causes→ cross-sensory recalibration
span.quote: As can be seen in Figure 3 , a larger shift in the auditory map occurs on postunity trials, suggesting that the perception of unity does influence the degree of subsequent recalibration.

span.label: teaching signal —operationalised-as→ self-supervised learning
span.quote: The visual signal appears to serve as a teaching signal for auditory modality, resulting in self-supervised learning of sensory representations.

span.label: reliability —causes→ teaching signal
span.quote: It seems that vision provided a teaching signal for auditory recalibration because the visual estimates were much more reliable (much lower variance in responses) ( Burge et al., 2010 ).

span.label: motor adaptation —contrasted-with→ cross-sensory recalibration
span.quote: However, an important difference between motor adaptation and the current example of sensory adaptation is that in the former, direct feedback can be used as teaching signal. Moreover, the motor system is expected to be highly malleable and dynamic (for instance, due to muscle fatigue), and thus, subject to adjustment.

span.label: plastic state —causes→ cross-sensory recalibration
span.quote: It is also conceivable that exposure to randomly varying discrepancies across trials in this experiment induced the nervous system to enter a “plastic state,” thus resulting a higher rate of recalibration than usual.

span.label: auditory–visual discrepancy —causes→ auditory localization
span.quote: The results show that shift in perceived auditory location is in the direction of visual discrepancy. This confirms that the observed change in auditory localization is driven by preceding auditory–visual discrepancy (or “error”), thus indicating visual recalibration of auditory space (rather than a bias toward the exposed absolute visual location).

span.label: Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks
span.quote: There was a significant effect of previous visual location on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 669, p = 0.000).

span.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
span.quote: The cyan star indicates that the shift is significantly different from zero [two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test with family-wise α = 0.05; significant after Bonferroni–Holm correction ( Holm, 1979 ) for each of the five tests: n = 134, 133, 136, 136, and 131, respectively].

span.label: multiple-comparison correction
span.quote: Stars denote data points that are significantly different from zero (corrected for multiple comparisons using Bonferroni–Holm correction).

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Unisensory auditory responses had an average SD of 6.0° (5.8, 6.5, 6.5, 6.0, and 5.2° for the five locations from left to right).

span.label: standard error of the mean
span.quote: The shift in perceived auditory location (mean ± SEM. across observers) as a function of location of the visual stimulus in the preceding V trial.

span.label: linear regression
span.quote: The observed auditory shifts are fitted well by a straight line with a positive slope ( p = 0.000) consistent with a recalibration mechanism, and inconsistent with the absolute visual bias mechanism.

span.label: Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test
span.term: Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test
span.quote: There was a significant effect of previous visual location on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 669, p = 0.000).

span.label: two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test
span.quote: There did exist a significant effect of previous AV discrepancy on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 1276, p = 0.000).

span.label: Bonferroni–Holm correction
span.quote: There did exist a significant effect of previous AV discrepancy on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 1276, p = 0.000).

span.label: SD
span.quote: Unisensory auditory responses had an average SD of 6.0° (5.8, 6.5, 6.5, 6.0, and 5.2° for the five locations from left to right). Unisensory visual responses had an average SD of 2.5° (3.3, 2.2, 2.0, 2.2, and 3.0° for the five positions from left to right).

span.label: A single 35 ms exposure to a spatially discrepant sound-and-flash pair shifted where the next isolated sound was heard, showing that auditory spatial recalibration needs no prolonged exposure.
span.quote: We show that in humans recalibration of perceived auditory space by vision can occur after a single exposure to discrepant auditory–visual stimuli lasting only a few milliseconds.

span.label: The shift followed the sign and size of the audio-visual discrepancy rather than the absolute position of the seen stimulus, identifying it as recalibration of the auditory map rather than a bias toward the visual location.
span.quote: The results shown in Figure 2 clearly indicate that the observed shift in the auditory map following AV trials ( Fig. 1 d ) is driven by the difference between auditory and visual positions (AV discrepancy, or error), rather then the absolute location of the visual stimulus.

span.label: Separately from recalibration, auditory localisation was pulled toward the absolute position of the visual stimulus presented on the preceding unisensory visual trial.
span.quote: First, we found that auditory responses are biased toward the absolute position of the preceding visual stimulus ( Fig. 1 b ).

span.label: The position of a preceding unisensory auditory stimulus had no significant effect on the current auditory judgement, arguing against a simple response bias.
span.quote: There was not a significant effect of previous auditory location on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 651, p > 0.05, n = 126, 126, 133, 132, and 135 for the five locations).

span.label: Recalibration was much stronger after audio-visual trials where the two signals were judged to come from one source, so perceived unity gates the size of the shift.
span.quote: As can be seen in Figure 3 , a larger shift in the auditory map occurs on postunity trials, suggesting that the perception of unity does influence the degree of subsequent recalibration.

span.label: Repeating discrepancies in the same direction accumulated a progressively larger shift, but at a decelerating rate, implying a decreasing learning rate rather than a fixed step.
span.quote: As can be seen in Figure 4 b , the degree of shift in the auditory spatial map increases with the number of repetitions of discrepancies in the same direction, but the rate of accumulation appears to slow down, suggesting a decrease in learning rate.

span.label: The recalibration was one-directional: no corresponding shift of the visual spatial map by sound was detectable.
span.quote: We also examined whether sounds provided a teaching signal for visual recalibration; however, no evidence of a shift in the visual spatial map was found in our data.

span.label: The effect weakened the further back in the trial history the audio-visual exposure lay, because intervening discrepancies pushed in other directions.
span.quote: As expected, the recalibration effect is degraded the further back we look in the AV history of trials, as intervening AV discrepancies counteract the effect.

span.label: auditory localisation shifted significantly with the location of the visual stimulus on the preceding trial
span.quote: There was a significant effect of previous visual location on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 669, p = 0.000).

span.label: no such effect followed a preceding auditory trial, which weakens a general response-bias account
span.quote: There was not a significant effect of previous auditory location on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 651, p > 0.05, n = 126, 126, 133, 132, and 135 for the five locations).

span.label: the audiovisual discrepancy on the preceding trial significantly shifted auditory localisation, and the shift grew with the discrepancy
span.quote: There did exist a significant effect of previous AV discrepancy on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 1276, p = 0.000).

span.label: on the subset where the two accounts predict opposite directions, the shift followed the discrepancy and not the absolute visual location
span.quote: The results show that shift in perceived auditory location is in the direction of visual discrepancy. This confirms that the observed change in auditory localization is driven by preceding auditory–visual discrepancy (or “error”), thus indicating visual recalibration of auditory space (rather than a bias toward the exposed absolute visual location).

span.label: recalibration followed a single 35 ms presentation with no feedback or reinforcement
span.quote: These results altogether indicate that cross-modal sensory recalibration can occur after a single presentation of stimuli lasting only a few milliseconds, and can occur in the absence of feedback or reinforcement. Thus, it appears that the nervous system is continuously engaged in cross-modal sensory calibration, even on the basis of a single exposure.

span.label: the shift was larger when the preceding audiovisual pair had been perceived as one event
span.quote: As can be seen in Figure 3 , a larger shift in the auditory map occurs on postunity trials, suggesting that the perception of unity does influence the degree of subsequent recalibration.

span.label: the effect degraded the further back in the trial history the preceding audiovisual trial lay
span.quote: As expected, the recalibration effect is degraded the further back we look in the AV history of trials, as intervening AV discrepancies counteract the effect.

span.label: the shift accumulated across consecutive same-direction discrepancies, at a slowing rate
span.quote: As can be seen in Figure 4 b , the degree of shift in the auditory spatial map increases with the number of repetitions of discrepancies in the same direction.

span.label: no shift of the visual spatial map was found, so the teaching relation is one-directional
span.quote: We also examined whether sounds provided a teaching signal for visual recalibration; however, no evidence of a shift in the visual spatial map was found in our data.

span.label: a single exposure produced about a 5% shift, against roughly 50% after hundreds or thousands of exposures in earlier work
span.quote: Our findings showing a significant and sizable (5%) shift in the spatial map following a single exposure raise the question of why a complete (i.e., 100%) and faster shift is not observed in these studies.

span.label: auditory localisation was about 2.4 times as variable as visual localisation, 6.0 against 2.5 degrees
span.quote: Unisensory auditory responses had an average SD of 6.0° (5.8, 6.5, 6.5, 6.0, and 5.2° for the five locations from left to right). Unisensory visual responses had an average SD of 2.5° (3.3, 2.2, 2.0, 2.2, and 3.0° for the five positions from left to right).

span.label: even the smallest discrepancy tested, 6.5 degrees, shifted the subsequent percept
span.quote: First, there does not appear to be a need for extended and substantial evidence of error for the mechanisms of sensory recalibration to be engaged. Even a single presentation at the smallest discrepancy tested (6.5°) can result in a shift of the subsequent auditory percept.

span.label: cross-sensory recalibration
span.quote: In contrast to motor or sensorimotor adaptation, which can be relatively rapid, cross-sensory recalibration (the change in an isolated sensory representation after exposure to conflicting cross-modal information) has been reported only as a result of an extensive amount of exposure to sensory discrepancy (e.g., hundreds or thousands of trials, or prolonged durations).

span.label: ventriloquist aftereffect
span.quote: It has been known that after repeated exposure to simultaneous but spatially discrepant auditory and visual stimuli, the perceived location of a solitary auditory stimulus is shifted in the direction of the previously experienced visual stimuli ( Canon, 1970 ; Radeau and Bertelson, 1974 ; Recanzone, 1998 ; Lewald, 2002 )—a phenomenon often referred to as the “ventriloquist aftereffect.”

span.label: N-back AV trial
span.quote: where the N -back AV trial refers to the N th AV trial before the A trial under consideration (i.e., with N − 1 intervening AV trials)

span.label: postunity and postindependence auditory trials
span.quote: Therefore, we calculated the shift in the perceived auditory location separately for two groups of auditory trials, a group in which the auditory response and visual response on the previous AV trial were within 0.5° of each other, and a group in which there was more than a 6° difference between the auditory and visual responses on the preceding AV trial.

span.label: shift in perceived auditory location (the dependent measure)
span.term: shift in perceived auditory location (the dependent measure)
span.quote: For each A trial, this is calculated as the response on that trial minus the observer's average response across all 15 A trials with that sound position (the given trial included in the average).

span.label: cross-sensory recalibration
span.quote: In contrast to motor or sensorimotor adaptation, which can be relatively rapid, cross-sensory recalibration (the change in an isolated sensory representation after exposure to conflicting cross-modal information) has been reported only as a result of an extensive amount of exposure to sensory discrepancy (e.g., hundreds or thousands of trials, or prolonged durations).

span.label: ventriloquist aftereffect
span.quote: It has been known that after repeated exposure to simultaneous but spatially discrepant auditory and visual stimuli, the perceived location of a solitary auditory stimulus is shifted in the direction of the previously experienced visual stimuli ( Canon, 1970 ; Radeau and Bertelson, 1974 ; Recanzone, 1998 ; Lewald, 2002 )—a phenomenon often referred to as the “ventriloquist aftereffect.”

span.label: shift in perceived auditory location
span.quote: We define the dependent variable in our analyses as the shift in perceived auditory location ( Fig. 1 b–d , ordinate). For each A trial, this is calculated as the response on that trial minus the observer's average response across all 15 A trials with that sound position (the given trial included in the average).

span.label: perception of unity
span.quote: Because we did not ask observers to report their perception of unity/independence, we indirectly identified these trials based on observer's spatial judgments.

span.label: auditory-visual spatial discrepancy on the preceding bisensory trial
span.term: auditory-visual spatial discrepancy on the preceding bisensory trial
span.quote: Therefore, auditory–visual spatial discrepancy varied from 0 to ± 26°.

span.label: stimulus type of the immediately preceding trial (auditory, visual or audio-visual)
span.term: stimulus type of the immediately preceding trial (auditory, visual or audio-visual)
span.quote: We examined observers' localization responses in A trials as a function of the type of stimuli presented on the immediately preceding trial.

span.label: shift in perceived auditory location
span.quote: We define the dependent variable in our analyses as the shift in perceived auditory location ( Fig. 1 b–d , ordinate).

span.label: starting azimuth of the response cursor, randomised to hold response bias constant
span.term: starting azimuth of the response cursor, randomised to hold response bias constant
span.quote: The position along the azimuth was randomized to minimize response bias.

span.label: order of the auditory and visual responses on bisensory trials, held constant within a session and counter-balanced across subjects
span.term: order of the auditory and visual responses on bisensory trials, held constant within a session and counter-balanced across subjects
span.quote: The order of these two responses was consistent throughout the session, and was counter-balanced across subjects.

span.label: perceived unity of the auditory and visual signals on the preceding AV trial
span.term: perceived unity of the auditory and visual signals on the preceding AV trial
span.quote: As can be seen in Figure 3 , a larger shift in the auditory map occurs on postunity trials, suggesting that the perception of unity does influence the degree of subsequent recalibration.

span.label: shift in perceived auditory location
span.quote: We define the dependent variable in our analyses as the shift in perceived auditory location ( Fig. 1 b–d , ordinate). For each A trial, this is calculated as the response on that trial minus the observer's average response across all 15 A trials with that sound position (the given trial included in the average).

span.label: AV spatial discrepancy
span.quote: Fifteen trials of the 35 stimulus conditions were presented in a pseudorandom order across trials. Therefore, auditory–visual spatial discrepancy varied from 0 to ± 26°.

span.label: perception of unity
span.quote: As can be seen in Figure 3 , a larger shift in the auditory map occurs on postunity trials, suggesting that the perception of unity does influence the degree of subsequent recalibration.

span.label: number of repeated exposures
span.quote: As can be seen in Figure 4 b , the degree of shift in the auditory spatial map increases with the number of repetitions of discrepancies in the same direction.

span.label: n = 146 — number of observers tested
span.quote: Observers ( n = 146; 100 females; age range, 18–35 years) sat 52 cm from a screen, with their chins rested on a chin-rest.

span.label: 35 ms — duration of the auditory (and visual) stimulus, i.e. the entire exposure that produced recalibration
span.quote: Auditory stimuli were ramped white noise bursts lasting 35 ms.

span.label: 0 to ± 26° — range of audio-visual spatial discrepancy produced by the five speaker and five visual locations
span.quote: Therefore, auditory–visual spatial discrepancy varied from 0 to ± 26°.

span.label: 5% — size of the auditory map shift after a single exposure, as a fraction of the experienced discrepancy
span.quote: Our findings showing a significant and sizable (5%) shift in the spatial map following a single exposure raise the question of why a complete (i.e., 100%) and faster shift is not observed in these studies.

span.label: 6.5° — smallest audio-visual discrepancy tested that still produced a shift in the subsequent auditory percept
span.quote: Even a single presentation at the smallest discrepancy tested (6.5°) can result in a shift of the subsequent auditory percept.

span.label: 6.0° — average standard deviation of unisensory auditory localisation responses
span.quote: Unisensory auditory responses had an average SD of 6.0° (5.8, 6.5, 6.5, 6.0, and 5.2° for the five locations from left to right).

span.label: 2.5° — average standard deviation of unisensory visual localisation responses, i.e. vision was the more reliable modality
span.quote: Unisensory visual responses had an average SD of 2.5° (3.3, 2.2, 2.0, 2.2, and 3.0° for the five positions from left to right).

span.label: p = 0.000 — significance of the effect of preceding visual location on the auditory shift
span.quote: There was a significant effect of previous visual location on auditory shift (Kruskal–Wallis one-way ANOVA by ranks test, df = 669, p = 0.000).

span.label: 35 ms — duration of the auditory and visual stimuli, and so of the single exposure
span.quote: Auditory stimuli were ramped white noise bursts lasting 35 ms. The visual stimuli were projected from a ceiling-mounted projector set to a resolution of 1280 × 1024 pixels onto the screen in front of the observers. The visual stimulus was a white-noise disk with a Gaussian envelope of 1.5° full width at half-maximum, presented so that the center of the disk was positioned at the center of one of the five (invisible) speakers. The visual stimulus was presented for 35 ms.

span.label: n = 146 — observers
span.quote: Observers ( n = 146; 100 females; age range, 18–35 years) sat 52 cm from a screen, with their chins rested on a chin-rest.

span.label: 0 to ± 26° — range of audiovisual spatial discrepancy across conditions
span.quote: Fifteen trials of the 35 stimulus conditions were presented in a pseudorandom order across trials. Therefore, auditory–visual spatial discrepancy varied from 0 to ± 26°.

span.label: 6.0° against 2.5° — average response standard deviation, auditory against visual
span.quote: Unisensory auditory responses had an average SD of 6.0° (5.8, 6.5, 6.5, 6.0, and 5.2° for the five locations from left to right). Unisensory visual responses had an average SD of 2.5° (3.3, 2.2, 2.0, 2.2, and 3.0° for the five positions from left to right).

span.label: 5% — shift in the spatial map after a single exposure
span.quote: Our findings showing a significant and sizable (5%) shift in the spatial map following a single exposure raise the question of why a complete (i.e., 100%) and faster shift is not observed in these studies.

span.label: 6.5° — the smallest discrepancy that still produced a shift
span.quote: First, there does not appear to be a need for extended and substantial evidence of error for the mechanisms of sensory recalibration to be engaged. Even a single presentation at the smallest discrepancy tested (6.5°) can result in a shift of the subsequent auditory percept.

span.label: 0.5° and 6° — the cutoffs separating post-unity from post-independence trials
span.quote: We left out the remaining A trials due to the possibility that small differences in reported locations may be due to motor errors; however, results remain qualitatively the same using other cutoff values.
